nodes.proof_latex:
The prime and lower-bound witnesses exclude $\ell=1,3$.  A prime
$\ell\ge5$ cannot divide $24$, so its image in $\F_\ell$ is nonzero.

nodes.title: I03: Euler mismatch in the correct range
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: If $\ell\ge5$ is prime and $\left(\frac{-r}{\ell}\right)=-1$, then the theta diagonal eigenvalue at $r$ differs from $\left(\frac{-24}{\ell}\right)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Invert $24$ in $\F_\ell$ and apply Euler's criterion and multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol.  The inert hypothesis changes exactly one of the two signs.

nodes.title: I04: identify the published grid normalization
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
The fixed published family has $G_1=0$.  For every $m>1$ coprime to $6$,
$G_m$ satisfies the published qualification predicate (and hence its
multiplier convention), and for every negative numerator index $r$ its
coefficient is
\[
 [q^{r/24}]G_m=
 \begin{cases}
 1&r=-m^2,\\
 -\chi_{12}(m)&r=-1,\\
 0&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Thus the numerator-indexed exponents, character, coprime range, and both
principal-part signs agree with the fixed convention used here.

nodes.title: I04: genuine grid construction
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
Given the exact published grid theorem, for every $m>1$ coprime to $6$ there
exists a unique qualified series with principal part
$q^{-m^2/24}-\chi_{12}(m)q^{-1/24}$.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the exact published modular-grid theorem when its multiplier and normalization match; otherwise start from $-\Theta j/\eta$ and eliminate successive principal parts by monic polynomials in $j$.  The absence of a holomorphic difference with zero principal part gives uniqueness.

nodes.title: Mock-form negative principal part
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
A coefficient series has the mock-form negative principal part if its
coefficient at index $-1$ is one and all its other negative-index
coefficients vanish.

nodes.title: I05: the actual mock series has its stated principal part
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
The integral coefficient series \(f\) has coefficient one at index \(-1\)
and has zero coefficient at every other negative index.
nodes.proof_latex:
Unfold the coefficient definition.  The exceptional branch is precisely
\(r=-1\), while the only other support branch requires \(r\ge0\).

nodes.title: I05: exact \(f\)-Hecke principal-part calculation
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
Let \(p\) be prime and nonzero in the coefficient field.  If \(f\) has the
mock-form negative principal part and the quadratic symbol satisfies
\((1/p)=1\), then
\[
 p^{-1}\bigl(f\mid T(p^2)-\chi_{12}(p)(1+p)f\bigr)
\]
has grid principal part
\(q^{-p^2/24}-\chi_{12}(p)q^{-1/24}\).
nodes.proof_latex:
Compute coefficientwise.  At index \(-p^2\), only the divided-index term
contributes; at index \(-1\), the middle Hecke term and the subtracted scalar
term combine to \(-p\chi_{12}(p)\); all other negative coefficients vanish.

nodes.title: I05: exact Legendre-square values
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
For every prime \(p\) and integer \(a\), the Legendre symbol satisfies
\[
 \left(\frac{a^2}{p}\right)=
 \begin{cases}0,&p\mid a,\\1,&p\nmid a.\end{cases}
\]
The same identity holds after casting into any coefficient field.
nodes.proof_latex:
If \(p\mid a\), use the vanishing criterion for the Legendre symbol.  If
not, apply the standard theorem that the character of a nonzero square is
one.

nodes.title: I05: actual \(f\)-Hecke principal part
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
After embedding the actual integral mock series into a characteristic-zero
coefficient field, for every prime \(p\), using the actual Legendre symbol,
the normalized series
\[
 p^{-1}\bigl(f\mid T(p^2)-\chi_{12}(p)(1+p)f\bigr)
\]
has the published grid principal part at index \(p\).
nodes.proof_latex:
Casting preserves the actual mock principal part.  A prime is nonzero in a
characteristic-zero field, so apply the exact coefficient calculation.

nodes.title: I05: Hecke qualification and principal parts
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
Given the exact citation-level qualification $\mathsf{I05Qual}(G)$, the
concrete normalized left and right sides form a value of the source-faithful
Hecke qualification package: all four sides qualify in the correct grid
spaces and both pairs have the internally computed common principal parts.
nodes.proof_latex:
Use the cited qualification for the two concrete left sides and the published
grid theorem for the right sides.  Compute the $f$ principal part directly.
For the grid side, split according to $p\mid m$, including the collision
$m=p$ and the convention $G_1=0$; multiplicativity and the square-one values
of $\chi_{12}$ and the Legendre symbol give exactly the principal part of
$G_{mp}$.

nodes.title: I05: identities from qualification data
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
Given concrete Hecke data whose two sides have the verified modular
qualifications and principal parts, uniqueness of the published grid proves
$\mathsf{HeckeSpec}(G,D)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the completion and shadow identity to the weight-$3/2$ Hecke image, use the eta Hecke eigenvalue, and compare the explicitly computed principal parts.  The uniqueness in the grid construction identifies both sides coefficientwise.

nodes.title: I05: actual source-faithful Hecke identities
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
The actual $f$ and published grid family, with the weight-$3/2$ Hecke operator
and source normalizations, satisfy the two Hecke identities in their valid
ranges.
nodes.proof_latex:
Construct the concrete qualification data from the completion/shadow and
principal-part calculations, then apply uniqueness of the published grid.

nodes.title: I02: corrected grid recursion
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: Let $\ell\ge5$ be prime.  Suppose $(m,6\ell)=1$ and $p\nmid6\ell$ with $p$ prime.  If $G_m$, $G_p$, and, when $p\mid m$, the earlier divided-index term $G_{m/p}$ lie in the required theta eigenspace modulo $\ell$, then $G_{mp}$ lies in that eigenspace modulo $\ell$.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the integral Fourier realization of the published grid to transport the characteristic-zero I05 identity first to an integral coefficient identity and then coefficientwise to $\mathbf F_\ell$.  Since $p\ne\ell$, Fermat's theorem makes the theta-cycle diagonal weight invariant under multiplication and division by $p^2$, so the Hecke operator commutes with theta.  The explicitly assumed earlier correction terms have the same eigenvalue; subtract them and cancel the nonzero scalar $p$ to obtain the assertion, never applying the step at $p=\ell$.

nodes.title: I06: grid theta support
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: If $\ell\ge5$ is prime and $(m,6\ell)=1$, then $G_m$ belongs modulo $\ell$ to the same theta eigenspace as $f$.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the integral grid realization to reduce both actual I05 identities coefficientwise.  Prove the prime base case from the reduced $f$-Hecke identity.  Then use strong induction on $m$: for composite $m=qp$ choose a prime divisor $p$, apply the induction hypothesis to $q$, $p$, and (when needed) $q/p$, and invoke the corrected recursion.  Coprimality descends to every divisor, so the argument yields only the claimed range.

nodes.title: I07: triangular auxiliary polynomial
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
For every $n=24k-1>0$, there is a unique monic integral polynomial $P_n$
of degree at most $k$ whose product $\eta P_n(j)$ has leading coefficient
$1$, no intervening polar terms, and coefficient $-a(n)$ at $q^{1/24}$.

nodes.title: I07: first auxiliary coefficient
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: For the polynomial from the triangular construction, the coefficient of $q^{1/24}$ in $H_n=\eta P_n(j)$ is $-a(n)$.

nodes.title: I07: actual auxiliary form
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: For every $n=24k-1>0$, the fixed $H_n$ satisfies $\mathsf{HnSpec}(n,H_n)$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Use the general E4 qualification of $\eta P(j)$ and the integral
unitriangular construction.  The solved rows give the leading term, the
vanishing low coefficients, and the first coefficient $-a(n)$.

nodes.title: I08: the genuine product has weight two
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: For $n=24k-1>0$ and $m>1$ coprime to $6$, the actual product $H_nG_m$ is weakly holomorphic of weight two, and its constant coefficient is the normalized three-term coefficient sum used in the duality calculation.
nodes.proof_latex: Combine the verified weights, multipliers, and principal parts of the two actual forms and multiply their Fourier expansions.

nodes.title: I08: coefficient duality
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: For $n=24k-1>0$ and $m>1$ coprime to $6$, one has $h_n(m^2)=-b_m(n)-\chi_{12}(m)a(n)$.
nodes.proof_latex: The genuine product $H_nG_m$ is weakly holomorphic of weight two.  Apply the general residue theorem to make its constant coefficient zero.  The two verified principal parts leave exactly the three displayed coefficients, and rearranging gives the identity.

nodes.title: Inert square-coefficient vanishing
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: If $\Can(\ell)$, $\Adm(\ell,n)$, and $(m,6\ell)=1$, then $h_n(m^2)\equiv0\pmod\ell$.
nodes.proof_latex: The exact coefficient reindexing turns canonicality into $f|U_\ell=0$.  Ahlgren--Kim gives the theta cycle, and the Euler mismatch kills $a(n)$.  Grid support kills $b_m(n)$; substituting both vanishings into coefficient duality proves the claim.  For $m=1$, use the verified coefficient $h_n(1)=-a(n)$.

nodes.title: I13: correct signed exponent decomposition
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex: For every $m\ge1$, the positive and negative parts of $e_n(m)$ satisfy $\mathsf{SignedExponentSpec}$.
nodes.proof_latex: Split on the sign of the integer $e_n(m)$.  The identities for positive and negative parts follow by integer arithmetic.  If $(m,6)>1$, the Kronecker character $\chi_{12}(m)$ is zero.

nodes.title: I21: injective Laurent substitution
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
For every $\ell,n$, every $h:\mathsf{AnalyticAdmissible}(\ell,n)$, and every
$d:\mathsf{LaurentSpec}(\ell,n,h)$, substitution
\[
  \F_\ell[T]\longrightarrow\F_\ell((q)),\qquad P\longmapsto P(d.t),
\]
is injective.
nodes.proof_latex:
The coefficient of $q^{-1}$ is one, so the $q$-adic valuation of $d.t$ is
nontrivial.  The valuation is trivial on the embedded coefficient field;
hence $d.t$ is transcendental over $\F_\ell$.  The standard
transcendence--evaluation equivalence gives injectivity.

nodes.title: I21: actual Laurent model
nodes.section: Sound analytic interfaces and the grid: I01--I08, I13, I21
nodes.statement_latex:
For every nonzero $\ell$, the actual eta quotient is the complex evaluation
of the integral Laurent expansion \(q^{-1}E_t^{\rm form}\), every coefficient
of its finite-characteristic model is the reduction modulo $\ell$ of the
corresponding coefficient of \(t_q^{\rm form}\), and that reduced model has
principal part \(q^{-1}-5+O(q)\).
nodes.proof_latex:
Use the analytic/formal identification for the complex equality and the
coefficient formula for Hahn-series mapping for coefficientwise reduction.

nodes.title: Level-six eta-exponent vectors
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: A level-six eta-exponent vector is a quadruple $(r_1,r_2,r_3,r_6)\in\Z^4$, indexed by the divisors $1,2,3,6$ of $6$.

nodes.title: Hauptmodul exponent vector
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The exponent vector of $t(\tau)=\eta(\tau)^5\eta(3\tau)/(\eta(2\tau)\eta(6\tau)^5)$ is
$e_t:=(5,-1,1,-5)$.

nodes.title: Eta weight numerator
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: For $e=(r_1,r_2,r_3,r_6)$, define $w_2(e):=r_1+r_2+r_3+r_6$, twice the eta-quotient weight.

nodes.title: I15: weight-zero calculation
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The fixed exponent vector satisfies $w_2(e_t)=0$.
nodes.proof_latex: Substitution gives $5-1+1-5=0$.

nodes.title: First Ligozat sum
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22

nodes.title: I15: first Ligozat congruence sum
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The fixed exponent vector satisfies $L_1(e_t)=-24$.
nodes.proof_latex: Direct integer arithmetic gives $5-2+3-30=-24$.

nodes.title: Second Ligozat sum
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22

nodes.title: I15: second Ligozat congruence sum
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The fixed exponent vector satisfies $L_2(e_t)=24$.
nodes.proof_latex: Direct integer arithmetic gives $30-3+2-5=24$.

nodes.title: Hauptmodul character parameter
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: Define the rational eta-character parameter $c_t:=2^{-6}3^{-4}=1/(2^6 3^4)$.

nodes.title: I15: square character parameter
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.proof_latex: Since $2^6 3^4=(2^3 3^2)^2=72^2$, the identity follows in $\Q$.

nodes.title: Level-six Ligozat cusp-order formula
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For a cusp denominator $c\mid6$, define
\[
 v_c(e):=\frac6{24}\sum_{\delta\in\{1,2,3,6\}}
 \frac{\gcd(c,\delta)^2r_\delta}{\gcd(c,6/c)c\delta}.
\]

nodes.title: I15: order at zero
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The cusp represented by denominator $1$ has $v_1(e_t)=1$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the four rational summands in the displayed formula.

nodes.title: I15: order at one-half
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The cusp represented by denominator $2$ has $v_2(e_t)=0$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the four rational summands in the displayed formula.

nodes.title: I15: order at one-third
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The cusp represented by denominator $3$ has $v_3(e_t)=0$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the four rational summands in the displayed formula.

nodes.title: I15: order at infinity
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The cusp represented by denominator $6$ has $v_6(e_t)=-1$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the four rational summands in the displayed formula.

nodes.title: General integral-curve function geometry
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Fix the neutral operations and predicates used for a rational function on an
integral curve: its divisor, the difference of two sections, absence of
interior zeros or poles, an integral unit expansion at a section, absence of
vertical components, and identification as a projective-line coordinate.
This structure contains no eta quotient or paper-specific application data.

nodes.title: E7 horizontal-divisor principle
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The general horizontal-divisor law says that on a good integral genus-zero
model, a rational function with no interior zero or pole and cusp orders
$+1,-1,0$ has divisor equal to the difference of its zero and pole sections.

nodes.title: E7 no-vertical-component principle
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The general spreading law says that a horizontal divisor which is the
difference of two disjoint cusp sections has no vertical component when the
function has an integral unit expansion at its pole section.

nodes.title: E7 integral degree-one principle
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The general degree-one law says that a rational function with horizontal
divisor the difference of two disjoint sections and no vertical component on
a good integral genus-zero model is a projective-line coordinate.

nodes.title: I15: no interior zero or pole
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: For every $\tau$ in the upper half-plane, $t_{\rm an}(\tau)\ne0$.
nodes.proof_latex: Each eta factor at $\tau,2\tau,3\tau,6\tau$ is nonzero by the standard Dedekind-eta theorem, so their indicated quotient is nonzero.

nodes.title: I15: conditional horizontal divisor
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For an E7 model whose four cusps are identified with denominators
$1,2,3,6$, if the fixed eta quotient satisfies Ligozat's hypotheses and the
chosen geometric model records that it has no interior zero or pole, then its
divisor is the difference $[0]-[\infty]$.
nodes.proof_latex:
E7 gives modularity and identifies each abstract cusp order with Ligozat's
formula.  The verified orders are $1,0,0,-1$; cusp exhaustiveness kills every
remaining order, so the general horizontal-divisor principle applies.

nodes.title: I15: formal integral unit expansion at infinity
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The independently constructed formal Euler product is literally
$q^{-1}u$ with $u\in\mathbf Z[[q]]$ a unit of constant coefficient one.
This does not identify it with the analytic eta quotient's Laurent expansion.
nodes.proof_latex:
Each stabilized Euler factor has constant coefficient one.  Their formal
product is therefore a power-series unit, and adjoining the computed net
$q^{-1}$ factor gives the displayed Laurent series.

nodes.title: Concrete actual integral unit expansion
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
An analytic function $f$ has the concrete integral unit expansion $u$ if
$u\in\mathbf Z[[q]]$ is a unit with constant coefficient one and, for every
$\tau\in\mathbb H$,
\[
 f(\tau)=q(\tau)^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}[q^n]u\,q(\tau)^n.
\]

nodes.title: I15: actual integral unit expansion at infinity
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The actual Mathlib eta quotient $t_{\rm an}$ has the concrete integral unit
expansion $E_t^{\rm form}$.
nodes.proof_latex:
The analytic/formal coefficient identification gives the displayed
convergent equality at every upper-half-plane nome.  The independently
verified formal calculation says that $E_t^{\rm form}$ has constant
coefficient one and is a unit of $\mathbf Z[[q]]$.

nodes.title: I15: conditional absence of vertical components
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For any E7 model and neutral curve-function geometry, a proved horizontal
divisor $[0]-[\infty]$ and an actual integral unit expansion at infinity imply
that the function has no vertical divisor component.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the general no-vertical-component principle to the good model, disjoint cusp sections, horizontal divisor, and actual unit expansion.

nodes.title: I15: integral degree-one divisor criterion
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For any E7 model and neutral curve-function geometry, a horizontal divisor
$[0]-[\infty]$ with no vertical component induces a projective-line coordinate.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the general integral degree-one principle to the good model, genus-zero fibers, disjoint cusp sections, divisor identity, and no-vertical-component fact.

nodes.title: I15: conditional integral degree-one coordinate
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For an E7 model, the four labeled exhaustive cusps, the fixed Ligozat
conditions and order identifications, a no-interior-zero-or-pole fact, and an
actual integral unit expansion at infinity imply that the fixed eta quotient
is a projective-line coordinate.
nodes.proof_latex: Derive the horizontal divisor, exclude vertical components, and apply the degree-one criterion.

nodes.title: I15: actual-expansion E7 coordinate chain
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Suppose an E7 model realizes its function type as analytic functions on the
upper half-plane and its expansion type as integral power series.  If its
fixed Ligozat quotient is identified with \(t_{\rm an}\), its geometric
predicates interpret pointwise nonvanishing and concrete integral unit
expansions, and the remaining E7 and cusp hypotheses hold, then the quotient
is a projective-line coordinate.  No separate integral-expansion premise is
required.
nodes.proof_latex:
Transport analytic nonvanishing through the no-interior interpretation law
and the verified actual integral expansion through the expansion
interpretation law.  Apply the conditional E7 coordinate theorem with these
two derived premises.

nodes.title: I15: standard-model application checks
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The permitted E7 boundary supplies the standard integral model of
$X_0(6)_{\mathbf Z[1/6]}$, its four cusp labels, the comparison of the
Ligozat quotient with the actual analytic eta quotient, the cusp-order
interpretations at denominators $1,2,3,6$, and the standard interpretations
of analytic nonvanishing and the concrete integral unit expansion.  It does
not supply a divisor or degree-one-coordinate conclusion.
nodes.proof_latex:
The cusp and quotient identifications are geometric comparison maps.  The
analytic and formal work now supplies the concrete expansion; the remaining
step is an interpretation law connecting it to the abstract geometric
predicate \(\mathsf{hasIntegralUnitExpansionAt}\).

nodes.title: I15: actual integral coordinate
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
From the E7 standard-model input, the fixed eta quotient induces the
degree-one integral coordinate
$X_0(6)_{\Z[1/6]}\simeq\mathbb P^1_{\Z[1/6]}$.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the verified conditional degree-one theorem after discharging every explicit actual-model premise.

nodes.title: Finite Galois polynomial descent
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $E/F$ be a finite Galois extension.  If every $F$-automorphism of $E$
fixes a polynomial $P\in E[X]$, then there is a polynomial $P_0\in F[X]$
whose coefficientwise image is $P$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Apply Mathlib's fixed-field theorem
\code{IsGalois.mem\_range\_algebraMap\_iff\_fixed} to every coefficient,
then use the coefficientwise characterization of the range of polynomial
mapping.

nodes.title: Integral polynomial descent from the fraction field
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $A$ be an integrally closed domain with fraction field $K$, and let
$L/K$ be a field extension.  If $P\in L[X]$ descends to $K[X]$ and every
coefficient of $P$ is integral over $A$, then $P$ descends to $A[X]$.
nodes.proof_latex:
For each rational coefficient, reflect integrality through the injective map
$K\to L$ and apply
\code{IsIntegrallyClosed.algebraMap\_eq\_of\_integral}; assemble the lifted
coefficients with \code{Polynomial.mem\_map\_range}.

nodes.title: I16: rationality of oriented class polynomials
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Given a finite Galois extension $L/\Q$ containing representatives of the two
actual oriented CM-value families, if CM reciprocity permutes each family,
then the two actual root products $A_n$ and $B_n$ have rational coefficients.
nodes.proof_latex: The reciprocity permutations fix both root products coefficientwise. Apply finite-Galois polynomial descent to each product.

nodes.title: I16: integrality of CM Hauptmodul values away from six
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Given the integral finite-Galois CM reciprocity datum supplied by potential
good reduction, every actual CM value $t(\tau_Q)$ occurring in $A_n$ or
$B_n$ is integral over $\Z[1/6]$.
nodes.proof_latex: Transport the root-level integrality statement from the finite Galois class field through its specified complex embedding, using its realization equality with the actual analytic value.

nodes.title: I16: monicity of the actual root products
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The actual polynomials $A_n$ and $B_n$, defined as finite products of factors $X-t(\tau_Q)$, are monic.
nodes.proof_latex: Each linear factor is monic, and a finite product of monic polynomials is monic.

nodes.title: I16: actual oriented class polynomials
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Given the integral finite-Galois CM reciprocity datum for the two actual
oriented CM-value families, there exists a
$\mathsf{ClassPolySpec}(n,P)$ descending the two fixed complex root products
to $\Z[1/6][X]$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Use finite-Galois reciprocity to obtain rational coefficients and
good-reduction integrality for every root.  Form the root products in the
integral closure, so all coefficients are integral over $\Z[1/6]$.
Intersect rationality and integrality by integral polynomial descent, then
transport monicity from the complex root products.

nodes.title: I17: coefficient reduction and algebraic-closure roots
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For prime $\ell\ge5$, the reduced polynomials satisfy
$\mathsf{RootReductionSpec}(P,h_6)$.
nodes.proof_latex: The localization map $\Z[1/6]\to\F_\ell$ exists because $6$ is invertible.  Map coefficients through this homomorphism.  Apply the field-theoretic criterion that two polynomials are coprime exactly when they have no common root in an algebraic closure.

nodes.title: I22: construct the four oriented class actions
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For squarefree $n\equiv23\pmod{24}$, given the permitted quadratic-order
domain theorem and fixed-orientation form--ideal-class equivalences, transport
of the regular proper ideal-class action induces simply transitive actions on
each of the four concrete quotients
$\mathcal Q_{n,1},\mathcal Q_{n,11},\mathcal Q_{n,5},\mathcal Q_{n,7}$.

nodes.title: I22: counts from the four oriented actions
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For squarefree $n\equiv23\pmod{24}$, given the permitted E8/E11
reduced-form equivalence and simply transitive E8 actions on the four concrete
oriented quotients, $\mathsf{ClassCountSpec}(n)$ holds.
nodes.proof_latex:
The pinned E8/E11 reduced-form classification identifies the concrete
reduced-form type of discriminant $-n$ with the proper ideal-class group of
$\mathbf Z[(1+\sqrt{-n})/2]$, including the boundary convention.  For each of
the four concrete orientation quotients, choose a base point in the permitted
E8 simply transitive action.  Sending an ideal class to its translate of that
base point is a bijection.  Taking cardinalities and composing with the
reduced-form equivalence gives all four equalities with $h(-n)$.

nodes.title: I22: actual class-number and orientation counts
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For squarefree $n\equiv23\pmod{24}$, given the permitted quadratic-order
domain theorem and the ordinary and fixed-orientation form--ideal-class
classifications,
$\mathsf{ClassCountSpec}(n)$ holds for the actual four oriented form
quotients.
nodes.proof_latex:
Apply the count-from-actions theorem to the four internally constructed
actions and the permitted E8/E11 reduced-form classification.

nodes.title: Class-polynomial degrees
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For a verified $\Z[1/6]$ coefficient descent of the actual four oriented root products, and every
good prime $\ell$, coefficientwise reduction preserves the degrees:
$\deg\bar A_{\ell,n}=\deg\bar B_{\ell,n}=2h(-n)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Each product contains two orientation sets.  Their cardinalities are $h(-n)$, and the degree of a finite product of monic linear factors is the number of factors.

nodes.title: Generic root specialization after coefficient descent
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $P\in\Z[1/6][X]$ become a finite linear-factor product after mapping to
an extension ring $R$.  For a residue map $R\to k$ compatible with reduction
$\Z[1/6]\to\F_\ell$, every root in $k$ of the coefficientwise reduction of
$P$ is the specialization of one of those algebraic factors.
nodes.proof_latex:
Map the coefficient-descent equality through the compatible residue
homomorphism, commute polynomial mapping with the finite product, and apply
the root criterion for a product of linear factors over a field.

nodes.title: I18: numerator root comes from an oriented factor
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For the actual coefficientwise-reduced numerator over an algebraic closure
of $\F_\ell$, a root is the specialization of one of the algebraic CM
values from orientation $1$ or orientation $11$ at a prime over $\ell$.
nodes.proof_latex: Transport the coefficient-descent equality to a common finite extension containing the CM values, specialize at a prime over $\ell$, and use that a finite product vanishes in a field only if one specialized linear factor vanishes.

nodes.title: I18: denominator root comes from an oriented factor
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For the actual coefficientwise-reduced denominator over an algebraic closure
of $\F_\ell$, a root is the specialization of one of the algebraic CM
values from orientation $5$ or orientation $7$ at a prime over $\ell$.
nodes.proof_latex: Transport the coefficient-descent equality to a common finite extension containing the CM values, specialize at a prime over $\ell$, and use that a finite product vanishes in a field only if one specialized linear factor vanishes.

nodes.title: I18: a common root gives one specialized level-six point
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Given a common finite-Galois realization, a compatible good-prime residue
specialization, and the integral degree-one coordinate realization on the
good fiber, a common root of the actual reduced $A_n$ and $B_n$ lifts to CM
factors of opposite orientation whose specialized level-six points coincide.

nodes.title: I18: specialize both CM actions
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Given the paper-specific map from a geometric class-polynomial collision to
two inert CM points with the same reduction, the permitted E8 theorems produce
a value of $\mathsf{CollisionSpec}$: both points acquire potentially good
reduction, their common reduction is supersingular, and both CM-order actions
specialize injectively.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply potential good reduction with level, Deuring's inert-reduction theorem, and injectivity of CM specialization to the two concrete CM points.

nodes.title: I18: common-root specialization
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Assume the standard E8 residue specialization, the integral degree-one
coordinate realization, and the interpretation of the two finite root
families as reductions of the corresponding inert CM points.  If
$\bar A_{\ell,n}$ and $\bar B_{\ell,n}$ have a common root in an algebraic
closure of $\F_\ell$, then $\mathsf{CollisionSpec}(\ell,n)$ holds.
nodes.proof_latex: Lift each root to its oriented CM factor.  The integral degree-one coordinate identifies equal reduced coordinates with the same geometric point of the integral model.  Apply potential good reduction and extension of prime-to-$\ell$ level structure.  Inertness gives supersingularity by Deuring, and specialization is injective on both CM orders.

nodes.title: Level-six orientation scalar
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: For an odd orientation residue $b$, define its scalar on the cyclic level-six subgroup by $s(b):=(b+1)/2\pmod6$.

nodes.title: Canonical quadratic element of an oriented form
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For a raw oriented form $Q=[a,b,c]$, define
\[
  \omega_Q:=a\tau_Q+\frac{b+1}{2}\in\C.
\]

nodes.title: I19: identify the canonical quadratic element
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For every raw oriented form of discriminant $-n$,
\[
  \omega_Q=\frac{1+i\sqrt n}{2}.
\]
nodes.proof_latex:
Substitute $\tau_Q=(-b+i\sqrt n)/(2a)$ and cancel the nonzero positive
leading coefficient $a$.

nodes.title: I19: conjugation of the canonical quadratic element
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: Complex conjugation sends $\omega_Q$ to $1-\omega_Q$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Use the explicit value of $\omega_Q$ and conjugate its real and imaginary
parts.

nodes.title: I19: trace of the canonical quadratic element
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: The reduced trace of $\omega_Q$ is $1$.
nodes.proof_latex: Add $\omega_Q$ to its conjugate $1-\omega_Q$.

nodes.title: I19: norm of the canonical quadratic element
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: If $n>0$, then the reduced norm of $\omega_Q$ is $(n+1)/4$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Multiply the explicit values of $\omega_Q$ and its conjugate and use
$(\sqrt n)^2=n$.

nodes.title: I19: quadratic equation of the canonical element
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
If $n>0$, then
\[
  \omega_Q^2-\omega_Q+\frac{n+1}{4}=0.
\]
nodes.proof_latex: Rewrite the reduced norm as $\omega_Q(1-\omega_Q)$ and rearrange.

nodes.title: Canonical generator of the negative quadratic order
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $\Omega_n$ be the distinguished generator of
$\Z[X]/(X^2-X+(n+1)/4)$.

nodes.title: I19: integral quadratic equation
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The generator $\Omega_n$ satisfies
$\Omega_n^2-\Omega_n+(n+1)/4=0$ in the canonical quadratic order.
nodes.proof_latex:
Apply the defining equation for the distinguished root of an
\texttt{AdjoinRoot}.

nodes.title: I19: specialization preserves the quadratic equation
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Every ring homomorphism out of the canonical quadratic order carries
$\Omega_n$ to a root of the same quadratic equation.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the ring homomorphism to the integral quadratic equation.

nodes.title: I19: trace after genuine specialization
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
If a ring specialization carries conjugation of $\Omega_n$ to quaternionic
conjugation, then its image has reduced trace one.
nodes.proof_latex:
Conjugation compatibility gives $\overline{\varphi(\Omega_n)}
=1-\varphi(\Omega_n)$; add the two terms.

nodes.title: I19: norm after genuine specialization
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Under the same conjugation compatibility, the reduced norm of
$\varphi(\Omega_n)$ is the image of the integral constant $(n+1)/4$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Rewrite the norm using conjugation compatibility, then rearrange the
transported quadratic equation.

nodes.title: I19: specialized norm is the canonical integer
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
The reduced norm in the preceding lemma is the canonical integer
$\lfloor(n+1)/4\rfloor$ in the target ring, independently of the
specialization homomorphism.
nodes.proof_latex:
Ring homomorphisms preserve integer casts, and natural-number division agrees
with integer division on nonnegative inputs.

nodes.title: I19: common norm of two genuine specializations
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Two conjugation-compatible specializations of the same canonical quadratic
order send $\Omega_n$ to elements with equal reduced norm.
nodes.proof_latex:
Both reduced norms are the same canonical integer
$\lfloor(n+1)/4\rfloor$ in the target ring.

nodes.title: I19: action specification from specialization maps
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Given two conjugation-compatible ring specializations of the canonical
quadratic order which realize the two specialized CM actions, together with
their geometric actions on the cyclic level-six subgroup, construct the
oriented action specification.  Its trace and common-norm fields are derived,
not supplied.

nodes.title: I19: scalar for residue one
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: One has $s(1)=1$ in $\Z/6\Z$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the definition.

nodes.title: I19: scalar for residue eleven
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: One has $s(11)=0$ in $\Z/6\Z$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the definition.

nodes.title: I19: scalar for residue five
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: One has $s(5)=3$ in $\Z/6\Z$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the definition.

nodes.title: I19: scalar for residue seven
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: One has $s(7)=4$ in $\Z/6\Z$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the definition.

nodes.title: I19: quadratic centralizer alternative
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: In a division ring with conjugation, if commuting elements $\alpha,\beta$ have reduced trace one and equal reduced norm, then $\beta=\alpha$ or $\beta=1-\alpha$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Trace one gives $\bar\alpha=1-\alpha$ and $\bar\beta=1-\beta$.  Equal norms and commutativity factor as
$(\beta-\alpha)(\beta+\alpha-1)=0$; the division-ring property yields the two alternatives.

nodes.title: I19: specialized actions do not commute
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For a collision from I18 whose specialized images satisfy
$\mathsf{ActionSpec}$, the two images $\alpha,\beta$ do not commute.
nodes.proof_latex: The four verified residues $b\equiv1,11,5,7\pmod{12}$ act on $C$ by $1,0,3,4$, respectively.  If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ commuted, the quadratic alternative would put $\beta$ in $\{\alpha,1-\alpha\}$, contradicting the disjoint numerator and denominator scalar sets.  The construction of the trace and norm identities remains to be supplied by the CM specialization.

nodes.title: I19: construct the actual specialized action data
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $S$ be a geometric CM specialization, let the E8 oriented quadratic
specialization supply genuine ring maps from
$\mathbf Z[X]/(X^2-X+(n+1)/4)$ together with its level-preserving subring
and scalar action, and let the two points of $S$ be identified with raw
oriented forms in the numerator residue family $\{1,11\}$ and denominator
residue family $\{5,7\}$.  Then these data construct an
$\mathsf{ActionSpec}$ for $S$.  Its trace-one and common-norm fields are
consequences of the ring specializations, rather than additional premises.
nodes.proof_latex:
Apply the action-specification constructor to the two E8 ring
specializations.  E8 identifies each specialized action with the image of
the canonical generator, proves compatibility with conjugation, proves
membership in the level-preserving subring, and supplies the scalar formula.
The transported quadratic equation and conjugation give trace one and equal
reduced norms for the two images.

nodes.title: I20: identify the preserving Eichler order
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: For any E9 model, a supersingular curve $E$ with a cyclic order-six subgroup $C$ has level-six Eichler preserving order by Arpin's theorem.
nodes.proof_latex: Verify that the specialized curve is supersingular and $C$ is cyclic of order six, then apply E9's exact order theorem.

nodes.title: I20: local covolume normalization
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: Given primitive local-index data recording indices $2$ and $3$, discriminant-$\ell$ maximal-order covolume, positive span index, and the exact covolume scaling law, the lattice spanned by $1,\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$ has covolume at least $6\ell$.
nodes.proof_latex: Substitute the recorded indices and maximal-order covolume into the scaling law; the positive integral span index is at least one.

nodes.title: I20: reduced norms of the four lattice vectors
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: If $N(\alpha)=N(\beta)=m$, then the squared-norm factors for $1,\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$ are respectively $2,2m,2m,2m^2$ in the Goren--Lauter normalization.
nodes.proof_latex: Use trace one, the common norm computation, and multiplicativity of reduced norm.

nodes.title: I20: apply the Hadamard bound
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: Noncommutation makes $1,\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$ independent, and the Goren--Lauter theorem bounds the square of their covolume by the product of the four verified squared norms.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the division-algebra independence lemma and instantiate the general four-vector inequality.

nodes.title: I20: level-six covolume inequality
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex: Given the E9 theorems, noncommuting actions of common reduced norm $m$, squared-norm compatibility, and primitive local-index data for their four-vector span, one has $6\ell\le4m^2$.
nodes.proof_latex: Arpin identifies the level-preserving ring as an Eichler order of level $6$.  The local index calculations at $2$ and $3$ give covolume $6\ell$.  Noncommutation makes $1,\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$ independent; apply Goren--Lauter to their lattice and use multiplicativity of reduced norm.

nodes.title: I20: actual E8--E9 volume inequality
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $S$, the E8 oriented specialization, and its two identified collision
forms be as in I19.  Let an E9 covolume model and general Eichler-lattice
arithmetic be given for the same division ring.  Suppose that the chosen
curve is the reduction of the numerator point, CM supersingularity implies
E9 supersingularity, its characteristic is $\ell$, the chosen subgroup is
cyclic of order six, the E8 level-preserving subring is the E9 preserving
order, and the arithmetic predicate for membership in an order agrees with
subring membership.  Then
\[
  6\ell\leq 4\left(\frac{n+1}{4}\right)^2 .
\]
nodes.proof_latex:
Construct the I19 action specification and hence derive noncommutation.
The two compatibility equalities transport E8's level-order membership to
membership in the actual E9 preserving order.  The defining quadratic
equation and conjugation compute both reduced norms as $(n+1)/4$; the
reduced-norm comparison transfers these values to the rational norm used by
the Eichler lattice.  The general E9 covolume theorem then gives the displayed
inequality.

nodes.title: Class-polynomial separation
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For the genuine descended class polynomials and the standard compatible
E8 residue/CM-action and E9 preserving-order models, if
$n\equiv23\pmod {24}$ and $(n+1)^2<24\ell$, then
$\bar A_{\ell,n}$ and $\bar B_{\ell,n}$ are coprime.
nodes.proof_latex: A common algebraic-closure root gives the specialized pair and the noncommuting actions.  Their common norm is $(n+1)/4$, so the volume inequality yields $24\ell\le(n+1)^2$, contradicting the strict bound.  The algebraic-closure root criterion gives coprimality.

nodes.title: Coprime low-degree Wronskian criterion
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
Over $\F_\ell$, if $A$ and $B$ are coprime, $A$ is monic, and
$0<\deg A<\ell$, then $\Wr(A,B)\ne0$.
nodes.proof_latex:
If the Wronskian vanished, coprimality would force $A'=0$.  In
characteristic $\ell$ the positive monic degree of such a polynomial is
divisible by $\ell$, contradicting the degree interval.

nodes.title: Wronskian nonvanishing
nodes.section: CM polynomials and separation: I15--I20, I22
nodes.statement_latex:
For the genuine descended class polynomials, if their coefficientwise
reductions are coprime and $0<2h(-n)<\ell$, then
$\Wr(\bar A_{\ell,n},\bar B_{\ell,n})\ne0$.
nodes.proof_latex:
The actual root products are monic of degree $2h(-n)$.  If the Wronskian
vanished, coprimality would make $\bar A$ divide its derivative.  The
derivative would be zero, forcing its positive monic degree to be divisible
by $\ell$, contradicting the degree interval.

nodes.title: Finite convolution constant term
nodes.statement_latex:
For a series whose pole order is at most \(n/24\), define the finite
coefficient convolution
\[
 \mathsf{FCT}_{n}(H):=\sum_{r=-n}^{1} H(r)a(-r).
\]

nodes.title: Finite constant term in the Stokes application
nodes.statement_latex:
\(\mathsf{CT}_{n}(H)\) is the sum of the two possible contributions to
\([q^0](Hf)\): the coefficient of \(H\) at \(-n\) paired with \(a(n)\),
and the coefficient at \(1\) paired with the unique negative coefficient
\(a(-1)\) of \(f\).

nodes.title: I09: only two constant-term contributions
nodes.statement_latex:
If \(H\) has the exact \(H_n\) Fourier normalization and \(n>0\), then
\[
 \mathsf{FCT}_{n}(H)
 =H(-n)a(n)+H(1)a(-1).
\]
nodes.proof_latex:
Every summand other than \(r=-n\) and \(r=1\) contains a coefficient of
\(H\) that vanishes by the verified low-index normalization.

nodes.title: I09: actual constant-term cancellation
nodes.statement_latex:
For \(n=24k-1\) with \(k>0\), the actual triangularly constructed
auxiliary form satisfies \(\mathsf{CT}_{n}(H_n)=0\).
nodes.proof_latex:
The leading coefficient of \(H_n\) is one, its index-one coefficient is
\(-a(n)\), and \(a(-1)=1\).  Hence the two terms are \(a(n)\) and
\(-a(n)\).

nodes.title: I09: finite-height Stokes application
nodes.statement_latex: For the actual pair $(H_n,\eta)$, the general finite-height Stokes theorem has the published nonzero shadow scale, the stated top-boundary error tends to zero, and its two surviving constant-term contributions are $a(n)$ and $-a(n)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Insert Bringmann's exact shadow normalization, compute every boundary term, and use the Fourier normalization of the actual $H_n$.

nodes.title: I09: specialized Stokes pairing
nodes.statement_latex: For every $n=24k-1>0$, the correctly normalized regularized pairing $\langle H_n,\eta\rangle^{\rm reg}$ is zero.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the finite-height Stokes theorem using Bringmann's exact shadow normalization.  The side boundaries cancel, the nonholomorphic top-boundary contribution tends to zero, and the remaining constant term is $\CT(H_nf)=a(n)-a(n)=0$.

nodes.title: I10: four-component Gauss sum
nodes.statement_latex: For $v=\mathfrak e_1-\mathfrak e_5-\mathfrak e_7+\mathfrak e_{11}$, the finite quadratic Gauss sum has the exact scalar required by the Weil representation at level $12$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the twelve residue classes directly, retaining the chosen square-root and sign convention.

nodes.title: I10: finite component Weil matrices
nodes.statement_latex:
For every scalar $c\in\mathbf C$, the level-$12$ normalized inverse Fourier
matrix fixes $c(\mathfrak e_1-\mathfrak e_5-\mathfrak e_7+\mathfrak e_{11})$,
and the diagonal quadratic $T$-matrix multiplies it by $e(1/24)$.
nodes.proof_latex:
Expand the normalized $S$-matrix on all twelve residue classes and apply the
verified Gauss sum.  For $T$, the four supported residues $1,5,7,11$ all have
square congruent to $1$ modulo $24$; the other eight components vanish.

nodes.title: Integral four-component coefficient series
nodes.statement_latex:
For an integral scalar coefficient series \(H\), define
\(\mathbf H(r,s):=H(r)\chi_{12}(s)\) on the twelve residue components.

nodes.title: Exact four-component Fourier-data predicate
nodes.statement_latex:
\(\mathsf{FourierData}(n,V)\) means that every component of \(V\) has zero
constant coefficient and that its only negative index is \(-n\), where its
coefficient vector is
\(\mathfrak e_1-\mathfrak e_5-\mathfrak e_7+\mathfrak e_{11}\).

nodes.title: I10: Weil generator transformations
nodes.statement_latex: The actual vector-valued form $\mathbf H_n=H_nv$ obeys the required $S$- and $T$-generator transformations.
nodes.proof_latex:
Combine the exact finite component-matrix calculation with the
scalar $S$- and $T$-transformation law of the actual $H_n=\eta P_n(j)$.

nodes.title: I10: vector principal part and constant term
nodes.statement_latex:
For \(n=24k-1\) with \(k>0\), the vector formed from the actual
triangularly constructed \(H_n=\eta P_n(j)\) satisfies
\(\mathsf{FourierData}(n,\mathbf H_n)\); equivalently it has zero constant
term and its only negative coefficient is the required integral vector at
index \(-n\).
nodes.proof_latex:
The scalar normalization has leading coefficient one at \(-n\), zero
constant coefficient, and no other negative coefficient.  Multiplication by
the explicitly integral twelve-component sign vector gives the assertion
componentwise.

nodes.title: I10: vector-valued Borcherds input
nodes.statement_latex: The fixed vector-valued form $\mathbf H_n$ satisfies $\mathsf{VectorInputSpec}(n,\mathbf H_n)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Evaluate the finite quadratic Gauss sum for the four-component vector.  The resulting matrices identify its $S$- and $T$-actions.  Substitution into the verified transformation law of $H_n$ gives the required Weil law, while the Fourier normalization gives the constant and principal parts.

nodes.title: I11: enumerate the four cusps
nodes.statement_latex: The cusps represented by $0,1/2,1/3,\infty$ exhaust the cusps of $X_0(6)$ with the conventions used in the Weyl-vector formula.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the squarefree-level cusp classification and check the four denominators dividing six.

nodes.title: I11: finite Atkin--Lehner eigenvalue table
nodes.statement_latex:
For $c=1,2,3,6$, let $\sigma_c$ be the permutation of $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ determined by
$\sigma_c(r)\equiv-r\pmod{2c}$ and
$\sigma_c(r)\equiv r\pmod{12/c}$.  Then the component vector
$v=\mathfrak e_1-\mathfrak e_5-\mathfrak e_7+\mathfrak e_{11}$ is a
$\sigma_c$-eigenvector with respective eigenvalues $+1,-1,-1,+1$.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the explicit multipliers $1,7,5,11$ modulo $12$ and enumerate the twelve components.

nodes.title: I11: finite theta-vector contraction
nodes.statement_latex:
For every four-component theta vector $\theta$ and $c\in\{1,2,3,6\}$,
contracting $v$ against the component permutation $\theta^{\sigma_c}$ equals
the corresponding sign $\varepsilon_c\in\{+1,-1,-1,+1\}$ times the
unpermuted contraction.
nodes.proof_latex: Reindex the twelve-term contraction by the verified involution $\sigma_c$ and use its eigenvalue on $v$.

nodes.title: I11: cusp-theta contractions
nodes.statement_latex: At each of the four cusps, the Atkin--Lehner action on $v$ and the theta contraction identify the vector-valued regularized pairing with the corresponding signed scalar multiple $\pm2\langle H_n,\eta\rangle^{\rm reg}$.
nodes.proof_latex: Use the finite contraction, the componentwise theta identity $\sum_r\chi_{12}(r)\theta_r=2\eta$, and bilinearity of the regularized pairing.

nodes.title: I11: all Weyl vectors vanish
nodes.statement_latex: For the four cusps of $X_0(6)$, every Weyl vector of the Bruinier--Ono lift of $\mathbf H_n$ is zero.
nodes.proof_latex: Compute the four Atkin--Lehner eigenvalues of the component vector and contract each cusp theta function to $\pm2\eta$.  The specialized pairing is zero, and the general Bruinier--Schwagenscheidt formula then gives each Weyl vector as zero with the correct normalization.

nodes.title: I12: signed Heegner divisor
nodes.statement_latex: For the actual vector input, the full interior divisor of the Bruinier--Ono lift is the signed sum $D_{n,1}+D_{n,11}-D_{n,5}-D_{n,7}$ at the actual complex Hauptmodul coordinates, retaining every point and its multiplicity.
nodes.proof_latex: Read the four orientation coefficients from the principal part, then apply them to the corresponding finite CM point divisors. The full numerator and denominator root multiplicities give the signed divisor.

nodes.title: I12: divisor of the class-polynomial quotient
nodes.statement_latex: Under the explicit rational-function divisor compatibility and zero-cusp-order inputs, the genuine quotient $A_n(t)/B_n(t)$ has the full divisor of its actual numerator roots minus its actual denominator roots, at every complex coordinate.
nodes.proof_latex: Embed the rational function field using the transcendence of the formal Hauptmodul. Cancellation preserves the signed root multiplicities. The descended coefficient polynomials map to the actual complex root products, so their full divisors agree.

nodes.title: I12: rational-function rigidity and normalization
nodes.statement_latex: Let $f,g$ belong to the rational function field embedded at the actual Hauptmodul. If their full divisors agree, their cusp orders vanish, and both Laurent constant coefficients are one, then $f=g$. Rigidity is not assumed for arbitrary formal Laurent series.
nodes.proof_latex: The constant coefficients exclude zero functions. Equal full root divisors give equal root multisets for the cross-multiplied polynomials. Polynomial factorization gives a nonzero rational scalar, and the two constant coefficients force it to be one.

nodes.title: I12: leading normalization
nodes.statement_latex: After base-changing the exact integral Euler-product Hauptmodul to $\mathbb Q((q))$, the coefficient of $q^0$ in the actual quotient $A_n(t)/B_n(t)$ is one; the coefficient of $q^0$ in the canonical stabilized Borcherds Euler quotient is also one.
nodes.proof_latex: Reverse the two monic equal-degree polynomials, cancel their common power of $t$, and evaluate the resulting power-series units at $t^{-1}$.  The principal part $t=q^{-1}-5+O(q)$ makes $t^{-1}$ have positive order, while both reversed polynomials have constant coefficient one.  On the Borcherds side, the canonical numerator and denominator power series both have constant coefficient one, and this remains true for their quotient after embedding into Laurent series.

nodes.title: I12: normalized Borcherds product identity
nodes.statement_latex: Assume the explicit analytic realization, full divisor and cusp compatibility, and genus-zero descent inputs. The descent domain consists of actual unitary meromorphic functions with convergent Laurent and cusp expansions; zero cusp orders imply rationality in the Hauptmodul. Then for squarefree $n\equiv23\pmod{24}$, the genuine descended class-polynomial quotient satisfies $A_n(t)/B_n(t)=\prod_{m\ge1}(1-q^m)^{\chi_{12}(m)h_n(m^2)}$ as a Laurent-series identity. The general analytic descent theorem remains a premise; rational-function rigidity is proved in Lean.
nodes.proof_latex: E6 first establishes zero Weyl vectors. The E5 product model is applied only on this qualified domain, where the cusp prefactor is absent; it supplies the analytic realization, full Heegner divisor and canonical Euler expansion. The cusp interpretation gives zero cusp orders. Apply the explicit genus-zero descent theorem to place the lift in the rational function field. The class quotient is rational by construction and has the same full divisor. The checked rational-function rigidity and leading normalizations give equality.

nodes.title: I14: actual stabilized Euler products
nodes.statement_latex: The fixed pair $(P_n^+,P_n^-)$ satisfies $\mathsf{EulerProductSpec}$.
nodes.proof_latex: For a fixed coefficient degree, factors whose index exceeds that degree contribute one, so a finite truncation computes the coefficient.  Apply the signed-exponent decomposition factor by factor.  Every truncation has constant term one, hence the denominator is nonzero.

nodes.title: Quotient derivative forces Wronskian zero
nodes.statement_latex:
Let $t$ be transcendental over a coefficient ring with nonzero derivative.
If
\[
  A(t)\,P^- = P^+\,B(t),
\]
$P^-\ne0$, and both $P^+$ and $P^-$ have zero derivative, then
$\Wr(A,B)=0$.

nodes.title: Canonicality forces Wronskian zero
nodes.statement_latex: If $\Can(\ell)$ and $\Adm(\ell,n)$, then $\Wr(\bar A_{\ell,n},\bar B_{\ell,n})=0$ in $\F_\ell[T]$.
nodes.proof_latex: Apply the specialized canonical-Euler-product Wronskian theorem.  For each Euler factor, either $\ell$ divides its index or inert square-coefficient vanishing makes its signed exponent divisible by $\ell$.  Frobenius makes both stabilized products have zero derivative.  Differentiate the normalized quotient identity, cross-multiply using the nonzero denominator, and cancel $\Theta t_q$.  Injective Laurent substitution forces the polynomial Wronskian to vanish.

nodes.title: First exceptional progression index
nodes.statement_latex: For prime $\ell$, let $k_\ell$ be the least $k\ge1$ for which $\left(\frac{1-24k}{\ell}\right)\ne1$.

nodes.title: Treviño interval bound
nodes.statement_latex: For every prime $\ell\ge10^{11}$, $k_\ell\le3.38\ell^{1/4}\log\ell+1$.
nodes.proof_latex: Before the first exceptional index, quadratic reciprocity turns the progression into consecutive values on which the genuine Legendre character is constant.  This character is nonprincipal, so the corrected Treviño theorem gives the stated length bound.

nodes.title: Explicit numerical cutoff
nodes.statement_latex: If $\ell\ge10^{11}$, then $81.12\ell^{1/4}\log\ell+24<\sqrt{24\ell}$.
nodes.proof_latex: Divide by $\sqrt{24\ell}$, prove both summands decrease for $\ell>e^4$, and verify the endpoint using $\log(10^{11})<26$, $(10^{11})^{1/4}>560$, and $\sqrt{24}>4.8$.

nodes.title: Minimal exceptional index is inert
nodes.statement_latex:
Assuming the corrected Treviño estimate E10, for
$n=24k_\ell-1$ and prime $\ell\ge10^{11}$,
$\left(\frac{-n}{\ell}\right)=-1$.
nodes.proof_latex: The numerical bound gives $0<n<\ell$.  Thus the exceptional Legendre symbol is nonzero, and minimality says that it must equal $-1$.

nodes.title: Minimal inert index is squarefree
nodes.statement_latex:
Assuming the corrected Treviño estimate E10, for
$n=24k_\ell-1$ and prime $\ell\ge10^{11}$, $n$ is squarefree.
nodes.proof_latex: If $u^2\mid n$ with $u>1$, then $u^2\equiv1\pmod{24}$.  Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol makes $n/u^2$ a smaller inert progression term, contradicting the minimality of $k_\ell$.

nodes.title: Class-number positivity
nodes.statement_latex: For squarefree $n\equiv23\pmod{24}$, $0<h(-n)$.
nodes.proof_latex: The principal form supplies a proper ideal class, and I22 identifies the reduced-form count with the ordinary class number.

nodes.title: Elementary class-number bound
nodes.statement_latex: For squarefree $n\equiv23\pmod{24}$, $h(-n)<n$.
nodes.proof_latex: A reduced positive form has $1\le a\le\lfloor\sqrt{n/3}\rfloor$ and $|b|\le a$.  Counting all possible pairs gives an upper bound below $n$ for $n\ge23$, and I22 identifies this count with the ordinary class number.

nodes.title: Small admissible discriminant
nodes.statement_latex: Every prime $\ell\ge10^{11}$ admits $n$ satisfying $\mathsf{SmallDisc}(\ell,n)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Take $n=24k_\ell-1$.  Squarefreeness and inertness follow from minimality.  The Treviño and numerical bounds give $n+1<\sqrt{24\ell}$.  The class-number estimate and $\ell>96$ give $0<2h(-n)<\ell$.

nodes.title: No large canonical prime
nodes.statement_latex:
Given the uniform E1--E11 literature ledger and the source-facing analytic
models for the published grid, Stokes pairing, and general Borcherds lift, if
$\ell\ge10^{11}$ is prime, then $\neg\Can(\ell)$.
nodes.proof_latex: Assume canonicality and choose the small admissible $n$.  The normalized product and Frobenius argument make the reduced Wronskian zero, while CM separation and the degree bound make it nonzero, a contradiction.

nodes.title: Public release proposition
nodes.statement_latex: $\mathsf{ReleaseStatement}$ is the proposition $\forall\ell,\ \Can(\ell)\leftrightarrow(\ell=5\lor\ell=7\lor\ell=13)$.

nodes.title: I23: discharge all paper-specific endpoint premises
nodes.statement_latex:
From a value of the uniform E1--E11 literature ledger and the source-facing
analytic model package one can prove $\mathsf{ReleaseStatement}$ without an
\texttt{InfiniteProductObstructionData}, arbitrary class-polynomial families,
a normalized-product premise, or a collision-data argument.
nodes.proof_latex: The internal constructions above produce the actual grid, $H_n$, Laurent Hauptmodul, class polynomials, Euler products, and CM specialization.  Large primes are excluded by the two Wronskian conclusions.  Ahlgren--Kim handles the remaining finite range, and Andrews proves canonicality for $5,7,13$.

nodes.title: Classification of canonical congruence primes
nodes.statement_latex:
For every value of the uniform E1--E11 literature ledger, every compatible
source-facing analytic model package, and every natural number $\ell$,
\[
\Can(\ell)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell=5\ \lor\ \ell=7\ \lor\ \ell=13.
\]
nodes.proof_latex: The public-endpoint proposition supplies the classification from exactly the literature record.
